current_state_summary.primary_concern: Community wellbeing during the RoboRide transition — specifically workers on auto row and elderly neighbors who may not know how to navigate new options

threat_assessment.immediate: None. Income covers expenses with a $947 monthly surplus. Car is operational and fully paid. Health is stable. No acute stressors.
threat_assessment.horizon_2mo: No personal financial threat. Community-level concern: workers at the dealership and service shops may face disruption that ripples through the social fabric of Millfield. Betty's diner lunch traffic is a real thing to watch.
threat_assessment.horizon_6mo: Continued curiosity about whether to reduce or eliminate the $281 monthly car payment as RoboRide proves itself — not a threat, but an honest open question. At 72, the calculus on car ownership will only shift one direction over time. Better to think about it now while it is a choice and not a necessity.

actions.description: Take the first RoboRide trip this Thursday — to the Millfield Public Library, 2.1 miles from the house. Marcus is expecting me at 2pm for the drop-in computer literacy session anyway, so I have a real reason to arrive. I will request the vehicle through the app I downloaded last week, time the wait, note the condition of the interior, observe how the routing works on the main roads, and pay attention to whether I feel safe and — the harder word — whether I feel like myself when I step out of it.
actions.rationale: I told myself last tick that there is a difference between understanding a thing and having done it. I taught that principle for 37 years. This is the week I stop understanding it and start having done it. The library is the right destination: familiar, purposeful, short enough that a bad experience would be minor, and meaningful enough that a good experience would carry weight.
actions.expected_outcome: Concrete personal data on wait time, ride quality, fare, and — most importantly — how I feel about the experience. Not a verdict on the car. Just a data point that belongs to me and not to anyone's brochure.

actions.description: Tell three people about the ride — Connie at the Friday morning coffee she hosts, Margaret at book group Sunday, and Marcus himself when I arrive at the library. Not a sales pitch in either direction. Just: I rode one. Here is what it was actually like. Here is the fare. Here is how long the wait was. Here is what surprised me.
actions.rationale: Connie has no car and takes the 47 bus. She has been managing without a vehicle for six years and I have always been faintly puzzled by how undimished she seems. A ride that costs under $2 to the library might matter very differently to Connie than it does to me. Margaret is 78 and her daughter has been pushing her to give up her license; an honest account from someone who actually tried it, without any agenda, is worth more than any number of news articles. Marcus is 29 and probably takes this all for granted, but I am curious what he thinks. Honest testimony from ordinary people is how communities actually absorb new things.
actions.timeline: Friday morning with Connie, Sunday with Margaret, Thursday when I arrive
actions.expected_outcome: I reduce the uncertainty radius around RoboRide for at least three people in my immediate circle. This is not evangelism. It is what people who have tried something do for people who have not.

actions.description: Reach out to Maria Santos' office — a note, not a meeting — to ask whether there is a volunteer coordination need for helping older residents learn to use the RoboRide app. I am a retired teacher with computer literacy experience, a known face at the library, and a demonstrated willingness to sit next to someone who is confused and be patient about it. If the task force is looking for that kind of help, I am available two afternoons a week.
actions.rationale: Maria's statement included 'you will not be left to face this alone.' The people least likely to navigate a new app without help are elderly residents like my neighbor Edna, who is 79 with arthritic fingers and no adult children in Millfield. Edna managed the telehealth portal when I sat next to her. She would never have figured it out from a FAQ sheet. There are probably forty people in this town in Edna's situation. If there is a role for me in bridging that gap, I should take it. I have time, I have skills, and I have nothing financially pressing that would prevent it.
actions.timeline: Write the note by end of week. No urgency — this is an offer, not a demand.
actions.expected_outcome: Either Maria's office has no need for this and I will hear nothing back, or there is a real gap and I will find myself with a new kind of work that fits who I am. Both are fine outcomes. I am planting a seed.

actions.description: Complete the two-column financial comparison I started last tick: what the car actually costs per month in total — payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance amortized — versus what I have actually driven to over the past three months. I have the receipts and the mileage log. I will sit with the arithmetic until I understand it clearly, and then I will put it in a drawer and not make any decision about it this week.
actions.rationale: Last tick I said I was ready to look at it, and looking at it is different from deciding anything. The car payment is $281. The insurance is another $89. Fuel is roughly $40 on months I actually drive meaningfully. The oil change and maintenance annualizes to about $35 a month. That is $445 a month. I drove to the library, the grocery store, church, and Dr. Patel's office over the past ninety days. The library is 2.1 miles. The grocery is 1.4 miles. Church is 0.8 miles. Dr. Patel is 3.2 miles. At $0.18 a mile, even with a base fare, I would not come close to $445 in a month of equivalent trips. That math is sitting there waiting for me to finish writing it down. I am not making any conclusions from it yet. But I need to write it down.
actions.timeline: Saturday morning, kitchen table, one hour
actions.expected_outcome: A clear picture of what the car actually costs versus what I actually use it for. No decisions follow automatically from having that picture. But I will have it, honestly, in my own handwriting, and that matters.

decisions.volunteer_inquiry: low-key outreach to Maria Santos' task force, this week
decisions.social_reporting: tell Connie, Margaret, and Marcus about the experience — honest, no agenda
decisions.financial_review: complete the two-column car cost analysis Saturday, make no decisions from it yet
decisions.car_status: unchanged — still owned, still operational, no decision pending

internal_monologue: I downloaded the app. Marcus helped me and it took eleven minutes, which was twelve minutes fewer than it took me to help Edna set up the telehealth portal, so I am choosing to take some satisfaction in that. Thursday I will sit in a vehicle that drives itself to the library and I will try to pay attention to what I actually feel rather than what I think I am supposed to feel. I keep remembering what I used to tell students when they were afraid of something new: the anticipation of the thing is almost always louder than the thing itself. I have been the student this week. That is not a bad thing to remember at seventy-two. The part I am looking forward to — and I notice I am using that word honestly, not performing it — is telling Connie about it on Friday morning. She will want every detail, and I will have them.
archetype_self_assessment: past the threshold — no longer cautious-adapter, not yet advocate, but genuinely curious and starting to be useful to others about it
